title: Basil and Llewelyn's Rolling Cart
markdown:
High up in the Moonfold Mountains, where the air smelled like crisp apples and stardust, lived a young wizard named Basil. He was not a wizard with a long swishy beard just yet. Basil had bright curious eyes that twinkled like fallen stars, and a heart as warm as his hearth fire. His pockets always seemed to hold a few shimmering pebbles, a forgotten feather, and perhaps a runaway spark or two that he would gently tuck back in.

And who was always with Basil? Llewelyn, of course. Llewelyn was not just any rabbit. He had the fluffiest tail in all the Moonfolds, a tail that wagged with pure wiggly joy, especially when there was moonlight clover to nibble. His long soft whiskers twitched with utter happiness as he ate. Sometimes he even did a little hop-skip-jump just because the clover was so tasty.

Basil loved his cozy cottage. The walls were painted the colour of pale honey. The fireplace crackled with friendly sparks that danced like tiny fireflies. Most of all, Basil loved to practice his magic. He would wave his wand—a twisty branch from near the Whispering Waterfall—and try to make his teacups dance a little jig or his socks fold themselves into neat little squares. Usually they just wobbled a bit, or a sock might try to escape under the sofa, which always made Llewelyn give a little chuckle-snort.

One evening, as the moon began to climb and paint the mountain slopes with long silvery shadows, there was a gentle tap-tap-tap at their little wooden door. It was Farmer Giles, their neighbor from just down the mountain path. Farmer Giles had kind eyes that crinkled at the corners when he smiled. Tonight his brow was furrowed. He fiddled with his hands, like a lost lamb.

“Oh, Basil, my boy,” he said, his voice a little shaky. “It’s my cart. My lovely apple cart. Every time I try to park it beside my barn, it just… rolls away! Down, down, down the hill it goes, like it’s trying to visit the badger sett!”

Basil tilted his head. “Rolls away? That sounds like a most peculiar puzzle, Farmer Giles.”

Llewelyn hopped closer. His fluffy white tail gave a concerned little flick. He nudged Basil’s hand with his soft nose, as if to say, We must help.

“It’s true,” Farmer Giles sighed. “I need to take my plump juicy cabbages and my sweet crisp apples to the market tomorrow morning. And I simply cannot have my cart rolling off into the deep woods. I’ve tried propping it up with stones. I’ve tried putting a big log behind it. It just keeps on going, bumpity-bump down the path.”

Basil stood up straight. His wizard’s heart felt a little flutter of eagerness. He loved solving puzzles, and this one sounded like just the right sort of challenge. “Don’t you worry for a moment, Farmer Giles. Llewelyn and I will come and have a look. We’ll go right now, before the moon gets too high and the shadows get too sleepy.”

Farmer Giles smiled, and a little of the worry melted from his kind face. “That’s very kind of you, Basil. It’s a moonlit wander through the fern-lit woods, mind you. Beautiful, with the moonlight dappling through the leaves, but it can be a bit twisty and turny.”

Basil grabbed his trusty wand. Llewelyn gave a happy expectant twitch of his ears. Off they went, hand-in-paw, into the whispering woods. The ancient trees stood tall and leafy, their branches like welcoming arms. Moonlight streamed down through the canopy, making the dewy ferns shimmer like tiny green jewels. It was wonderfully peaceful, with only the gentle chirping of sleepy crickets and the soft rustle of leaves underfoot.

They walked and walked, following the little winding mountain path. Llewelyn hopped with a cheerful rhythm ahead of Basil, his twitching nose sniffing the cool damp air. Basil kept his keen wizard’s eyes open, looking for anything unusual, anything that might make a cart decide to take a spontaneous slide down a hill.

As they rounded a bend where the ferns grew particularly thick and dewy, their silvery fronds unfurling like tiny fans, they heard a soft melodious humming. There, sitting on a mossy log that looked as if it were covered in velvet, was a lady with kind knowing eyes and a big woven basket overflowing with colourful herbs—some feathery, some curly, some with tiny bright flowers. She looked up from her work and smiled, a smile as warm as a sunbeam.

“Hello there, young travellers,” she said, her voice as gentle as a summer breeze. “You two look like you’re on a special mission. Are you searching for something important?”

Basil blinked, a little surprised but not at all worried. He had met friendly folk in the woods before. “We are. We’re helping Farmer Giles because his cart keeps rolling downhill. It’s a big problem.”

The lady chuckled, a sound like little bells. “Ah, yes. Farmer Giles’s cart. That’s a curious thing that happens sometimes. I’m Willow, by the way.” She smoothed her apron. “I know a little bit about keeping things from rolling when they ought to stay put. I’ve lived in these woods for a very long time, you see.”

Llewelyn’s tail gave a hopeful wag. His whiskers practically vibrated with anticipation.

Willow reached into her basket, fingers rustling through fragrant leaves and dried flowers. “That’s the curious thing about carts, and wheels, and all sorts of things that go around,” she said, picking out a tiny silvery twig that seemed to glow faintly in the moonlight. “Sometimes they just get a little bit… unfastened. There’s a tiny bolt on Farmer Giles’s cart wheel that’s just come loose. It’s so small, so shy, you’d hardly see it unless you were looking very, very closely.”

Basil’s eyes widened. “A loose bolt. Of course. That makes perfect sense.” He imagined a tiny bolt, like a little silver bug, letting go.

Willow held out the silvery twig. “This is a moonpetal twig. The leaves from this twig, when dried and sprinkled around a loose bolt, have a special property. They will help it tighten up, strong and firm, with just a little bit of moon magic to guide them. A very gentle kind of magic, but very effective.”

With Willow leading the way, they all went back along the path to Farmer Giles’s cart. The cart sat there, looking perfectly ordinary in the moonlight. But Basil now knew about the secret shy loose bolt. Willow carefully sprinkled a pinch of the dried moonpetal leaves all around the base of the bolt, and Basil gave his wand a tiny encouraging flick, whispering a gentle word of help.

With a soft little shhhh, almost like a sigh of contentment, the wheel seemed to settle deeper into the ground. The cart stood perfectly still. It did not budge an inch, not even when Llewelyn nudged it with his nose. It was as steady as a mountain.

Farmer Giles, who had followed them quietly, clapped his hands softly together, the sound like dry leaves rustling. “It worked! Oh, it really worked! Thank you, Basil. Thank you, Llewelyn. And thank you, Willow. You’ve saved my cabbages and my apples, and my market day.”

Willow smiled, her eyes twinkling. “Happy to help keep things on the path, Farmer Giles.”

They all stood for a moment, admiring the steady cart, then looking up at the bright friendly moon, and then at each other. Farmer Giles insisted they come back to his warm farm for a mug of milky tea. Llewelyn even got a special little saucer of fresh sweet milk, which he lapped up with great delight.

Basil sipped his tea, warmth spreading through him, with Llewelyn curled contentedly at his feet, already dreaming of moonlight clover. The cart, down by the barn, did not roll. Tomorrow’s apples would still be there in the morning.
characters: Basil (young wizard of the Moonfold Mountains), Llewelyn (fluffiest-tailed rabbit of moonlight clover)
